newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: New S.African competition law seen tabled in 1997.
newsitem.headline: New S.African competition law seen tabled in 1997.

text.p: New competition legislation would be tabled in parliament in the first part of 1997, South African Trade and Industry Ministry Minister Alec Erwin said at the weekend.
Speaking at a National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) press conference, Erwin said a competition policy discussion document would be presented for debate at Nedlac in mid-October.

"We should try and complete our Nedlac discussions some time by the end of January and then go through the cabinet cycle and the legislative cycle, so that we can table legislation in the first part of next year," he said.
He said parallel to the discussions at Nedlac -- which groups government, business and labour -- a legal brief on competition would be drawn up by the Department of Trade and Industry.
This would then be presented to the portfolio committee in parliament where the public would be able to submit comments on the legislation.

Stef Naude, chairman of Business South Africa, said while participants at Nedlac's policy discussion meeting on Friday had agreed on how the debate on competition policy would proceed from now, its contents were still up for debate.
"The whole question of what is going to be in that bill is a matter for negotiation," Naude said.
Business has opposed the forced break up of South Africa's conglomerates which it believes will reduce the country's international competitiveness.

The first draft of a competition policy was handed to former Trade and Industry Minister Trevor Manuel in September 1995, but was rejected by Manuel who said he wanted a bill that contributed to growth and development.
Erwin said in May that he hoped new competition legislation would be presented late this year.
But work pressures had resulted in government making slow progress on the legislation.
"It has not been our partners that have slowed this down, it is us and we will put it through in October. The reason for the delay is only work pressure rather than anything else," he said.
